description: One-dimensional layouts: rows, columns, alignment, and items that grow.

screens.body:
Flexbox arranges items in a single line — a row or a column. You turn it on with display: flex on the PARENT, and its children (the flex items) line up automatically.

It's the tool for navbars, button rows, card lists, and anything that should sit side by side and share space nicely.

Think of the parent as a manager: it decides the direction, the alignment, and how extra space gets shared.

check.question: Where do you put display: flex?

screens.heading: Flexbox arranges things in a line
screens.keyPoint: display: flex on the parent; children become flex items.

screens.body:
flex-direction sets the line's direction: row (left to right, the default) or column (top to bottom).

row-reverse and column-reverse flip the order — same items, reversed line.

This one property turns a horizontal navbar into a vertical stack. Direction first, everything else follows.

check.question: How do you stack flex items vertically?

screens.heading: Direction: row or column
screens.keyPoint: flex-direction: row or column sets the line.

screens.body:
justify-content aligns items along the MAIN axis — the direction of the line. In a row, that's horizontal.

flex-start packs items at the start, center centers them, flex-end packs them at the end. space-between pushes the first and last to the edges; space-around adds even breathing room.

It's the fastest way to space out a navbar or center a row of buttons.

options: Along the main axis (the line's direction)
check.question: What does justify-content control?

screens.heading: Main-axis alignment: justify-content

screens.body:
align-items aligns items along the CROSS axis — perpendicular to the line. In a row, that's vertical.

The default is stretch: items grow to fill the container's height. center lines them up in the middle; flex-start and flex-end pin them top or bottom.

justify-content and align-items together handle nearly all alignment you'll ever need.

options: Perpendicular to the line (vertical in a row)
check.question: What does align-items control?

screens.heading: Cross-axis alignment: align-items

screens.body:
flex controls how items grow and shrink to fill space. flex: 1 means "take an equal share of the leftover room."

Give one item flex: 2 and a sibling flex: 1, and the first gets twice the extra space — like splitting a pizza 2-to-1.

Under the hood, flex is shorthand for grow, shrink, and basis, but flex: 1 covers most real cases.

options: They split the leftover space equally
check.question: Two items, both flex: 1, in a 300px row. What happens?

screens.heading: Growing and shrinking: flex
screens.keyPoint: flex: 1 = take an equal share of leftover space.

screens.body:
By default, flex items squeeze onto one line even if they overflow. flex-wrap: wrap lets them flow onto the next line instead.

gap adds space between items — cleaner than margins, because it doesn't add stray space at the edges.

Wrap + gap is the recipe for responsive card grids that reflow as the screen shrinks.

options: They wrap onto the next line
check.question: With flex-wrap: wrap, what do overflowing items do?

screens.heading: Wrapping: flex-wrap
screens.keyPoint: flex-wrap: wrap + gap = reflowing card rows.

screens.body:
Centering used to be CSS's hardest problem. Flexbox made it three lines:

display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; — and anything inside sits dead center, both directions.

Memorize this snippet. You'll use it for hero sections, modals, empty states, and loading screens for the rest of your career.

options: display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;
check.question: Which snippet perfectly centers an item?

screens.heading: Centering the easy way
